line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Be3 Bg7 c3 Nf6
teaches: When your opponent reinforces one piece with a pawn move that steals a square from another, count the defenders of their centre again — the pawn move often costs more than it saves. A move that neither develops nor defends the pawn that matters is an invitation to attack that pawn one more time.
explains: The pawn move to c3 propped up the knight but took the c3 square away from the queenside knight — the natural defender of the pawn on e4. The knight comes to f6 attacking that pawn, and there is no longer a clean way to add a defender.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Be3 Bg7 c3 Nf6 Bb5 Nxe4 Bxc6 dxc6
teaches: When several recaptures are possible, prioritise piece placement and activity over pawn structure. The recapture that opens lines for your unmoved pieces is usually worth a small structural concession — pieces win games while structure is being admired.
explains: Taking with the d-pawn opens the queen's file: the path from d8 down to the knight on d4 is clear where a pawn stood a move ago, and the bishop on c8 has its diagonal too. The alternative capture kept the prettier pawns and left both of those pieces staring at their own pawn.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Be3 Bg7 c3 Nf6 Bb5 Nxe4 Bxc6 dxc6 O-O O-O Nd2 Nf6
teaches: A retreat that begins a redeployment is a retreat in name only. When trading would relieve your opponent's cramped pieces, step back instead and point the piece at its next post — keeping the pieces on is itself a way of making a passive position hard to breathe in.
explains: The knight steps back to f6 rather than trading itself for the passive knight, and from here it looks at two forward posts at once: it takes d5 under control in the centre and g4 beside the enemy king's position. The piece spent one move and gained two futures.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Be3 Bg7 c3 Nf6 Bb5 Nxe4 Bxc6 dxc6 O-O O-O Nd2 Nf6 Nc4 Qc7
teaches: Look for the queen move that does two jobs from one square: eye a distant weakness and support the pieces' next jumps. The best queen squares early in the middlegame are usually the quiet ones a knight cannot reach, where the queen pressures without being pressured.
explains: From c7 the queen attacks the pawn on h2 down a completely open diagonal, and the same square supports the knight's leap toward g4 next. Nothing attacks the queen on c7, and everything she looks at has to be minded.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Be3 Bg7 c3 Nf6 Bb5 Nxe4 Bxc6 dxc6 O-O O-O Nd2 Nf6 Nc4 Qc7 Qf3 Nd5 Rad1 e5
teaches: Keep the tension until your pieces are placed, then let the central pawns roll. A pawn push that arrives hitting a piece starts the whole advance with a gained move, and each pawn that follows walks into space the first one cleared.
explains: The pawn steps to e5 and attacks the knight on d4 directly, so the central advance begins on the opponent's clock. It also takes f4 in hand for the pawn behind it — the plan is e5, then f5, then the further push, and this first step pays for itself.
